title: How To Handle A Student Who Does Zero Work https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2022/02/18/how-to-handle-a-student-who-does-zero-work/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the instinct to intervene — kneeling beside a non-working student, asking why, offering help, or threatening consequences — arguing that this well-meaning attention actually entrenches resistance. He frames chronic non-work as a bid for control and self-determinism: students who refuse to work are exercising the one choice still fully theirs, and adult pressure only strengthens their need to resist. His counterintuitive recommendation is to do nothing directly about the refusal itself, instead removing the pressure that triggers it while doubling down on trusting rapport and compelling, expertly delivered lessons. He argues the deeper fix is systemic: teachers must take responsibility for teaching engaging content and then hand full responsibility for listening, learning, and working over to students, combined with real freedom to succeed or fail. Rewards and threats produce only temporary compliance; removing the need to resist is what produces lasting, self-directed work.
points: Kneeling down to question, cajole, or bargain with a non-working student typically entrenches their resistance rather than resolving it.
Chronic work refusal is often a bid for control and self-determinism, not laziness or defiance for its own sake.
The recommended response is to stop pressuring the student directly and instead remove the pressure that provokes resistance.
Compelling, expertly delivered lessons combined with genuine freedom to choose (and face natural consequences) motivate work more than rewards or threats.
Sustainable motivation comes from shifting full responsibility for learning onto students once the teacher has done their job of teaching well.
quotes: Because students who don’t work are seeking control, first and foremost. They’re feeling as if they’re losing their ability to make their own choices. And not doing their work is something they alone can decide.
Nothing. Yes, really. I know it sounds blasphemy, but letting them be is the best thing you can do for them. The choice to work must be theirs.
And not in the phony way we can sometimes get them moving by offering rewards or threatening punishment—which doesn’t last. But in a way that is real and sustaining.
Remove their need to resist and give them their control and freedom of choice back. It’s that simple.
It’s not the student. It’s us. We have to do better. We have to know and understand what really motivates students instead of assuming that they’re the problem.
They want to be stirred and challenged, if only you’ll give it them, along with the one thing what we all desire deep down.
